abstract: This study used a randomized field experiment on Facebook during the 2020 US election to examine the effects of exposure to reshared content. Consenting US-based users were randomly assigned to receive feeds without any reshares over a three-month period. Removing reshares substantially reduced exposure to political news—including content from untrustworthy sources—and lowered engagement, but did not produce detectable changes in downstream political beliefs or opinions.
key_claims: Reshared content on Facebook amplifies users' exposure to political news, including content from untrustworthy sources.
Despite amplifying political content exposure, removing reshares does not detectably affect users' political beliefs or opinions.
Reshares are a significant driver of engagement (clicks and reactions) with political and partisan news.
methods: Randomized controlled experiment conducted on Facebook during the 2020 US election.
Consenting US-based users randomly assigned to a treatment condition with feeds containing no reshared content.
Intervention sustained over a three-month period.
Measurement of exposure to political news, exposure to untrustworthy sources, clicks, reactions, and partisan news clicks, alongside survey-based measures of beliefs and opinions.
findings: Removing reshared content substantially decreased the amount of political news to which users were exposed.
Exposure to content from untrustworthy sources decreased when reshares were removed.
Overall clicks and reactions decreased under the no-reshare condition.
Partisan news clicks were reduced when reshares were removed.
No detectable effect on political beliefs or opinions was observed despite reduced exposure and engagement.
contributions: Provides causal evidence on the role of reshares in amplifying political news exposure on a major social media platform.
Demonstrates a dissociation between changes in content exposure/engagement and changes in political attitudes.
Contributes large-scale experimental evidence to debates about social media's influence on political outcomes during a major election.
framing: The paper is situated within research on social media's effects on political behavior, misinformation, and democratic outcomes, addressing whether platform design features like resharing shape political beliefs. It engages debates about the persuasive power of online exposure versus its limited attitudinal impact.
